reasons: Anchor (Lazar Parp. p.2218 w1-w2) says the teacher's doctrine was sweet 'according to the word of the prophet David, than the honeycomb' (mełu): an explicit quotation of Psalm 19:10/119:103, so derivative from the Bible. Il. 1.249 (Nestor: speech sweeter than honey flowed from his tongue) is checked as quoted; Clement Paed. 1.6.51 s3 quotes Homer and in s4 sets it beside prophetic 'above honey and honeycomb', a learned Greek-Christian conflation, not an independent witness. Only the honey noun is cognate (mełr ~ meli < *melit-); the adjective and speech noun do not match. Honey-sweet speech is a widespread figure.
known: Honey-sweet speech (Il. 1.249; Vedic madhu-) is a well-known figure in IE poetics; the Armenian here is Biblical.

reasons: Anchor (Movses Khor. p.1830, Vahagn birth song) checked: Vahagn 'had fire hair (hur her), flame beard (bocʻ ... mawrus)' and was blond (xartеaš), born from flame out of a reed in the sea. RV 10.96.8a háriśmaśāruḥ hárikeśaḥ (Indra, tawny-bearded, tawny-haired) and RV 5.7.7c híriśmaśruḥ (Agni, golden-bearded), 3.14.1d śocíṣkeśaḥ (Agni, flame-haired) say what the lead says. mawrukʻ ~ śmáśru- < *smoḱru- is the standard etymology (Martirosyan s.v. mawrukʻ, de Lagarde; the vocalism a is disputed but the equation is accepted). Only one cognate element: hair words (her vs kéśa) and colour/fire words are not cognate, and the luminous hair+beard pair is distributed over several Vedic lines and gods. The Agni partners fit best (fire god born in the waters), which strengthens context, but Iranian mediation (Vahagn < Vərəθraγna) and generic luminous-deity description remain possible. Defensible but not compelling.
known: The Vahagn birth song has long been compared with Vedic Agni's birth from the waters/reed; the fiery beard detail is part of that discussion.

reasons: Anchor (Lazar p.2359, word 57422) checked: 'for a brave man, rather than living many hours in disgrace, it is better to make known one day the worth of himself and die'. Il. 15.511 (Ajax: better once and for all to perish or to live than to be ground down long in dread battle) and Laxdaela 166r:4 'betra ... skjóta sǿmð en langa svívirðing' are checked and match thematically. As the lead itself says, no cognate lexemes carry the figure (ayr 'man' is incidental); short-glory vs long-shame is a widespread heroic gnome. Not phraseology.
known: The choice of short glory over long life (Achilles' choice; Beowulf 2890-91) is a well-known theme.

reasons: Anchor (Lazar p.2355) checked: that the king 'see with his own eyes (ačʻawkʻ), hear with his own ears (akanǰawkʻ), speak with his own mouth' and not with others'. Theog. 701 'to see with the eyes and hear the sound with the ears' and AVŚ 9.4.34 'hears good with his two ears (karṇābhyām)' checked. Instrumental eyes-see / ears-hear is a universal physiological pairing. ačʻkʻ < *h3okw- is sound, but akanǰ is not securely from *h2ous- (Martirosyan s.v. akanǰ: unclear, many proposals, ǰ taken over from ačʻ); Vedic karṇa is a different word. The Armenian is a political petition (direct royal knowledge), unlike the Hesiodic cosmic battle.

Anchor (Agathangelos p.1659, vision) checked: 'Behold the doors of heaven (drunkʻ erknicʻ) are opened, let there be no obstacle for people to go up'. RV 1.48.15b: Dawn, when you open the two doors of heaven with your light, is accurate. dur̄n ~ dvā́r- < *dhwer- is a good cognate, but erkin is not from *diw- and the predicate differs. In a Christian martyr vision the 'opened doors/gate of heaven' is a Biblical expression (Ps 78:23, Gen 28:17, Rev 4:1), so the Armenian is derivative.
known: Doors of heaven (dvā́rau diváḥ) is a known Vedic figure.

reasons: Anchor (Movses, Geography p.2156) checked: a spring by which the gods (dikʻn) swear because of its extreme cold, named Stełos. This is the Styx, taken over by name in a geography derived from Greek sources; Il. 15.37-38 and Od. 5.185-186 (Styx water, greatest oath of the gods) checked. Derivative from Greek. The cognate statement is also wrong: Arm. dikʻ (*deiw-) is not cognate with Greek theos (< *dhh1s-o-).
known: The Styx oath of the gods is the well-known Greek motif.

reasons: Anchor (Lazar p.2316 w3) checked: by attacking now you finish a great task easily and, having gained a good name (law anun), we will find honours and gifts from the king of kings. Thucydides 4.87.6 (to put the finest name on the whole city) checked. anun ~ onoma < *h1nomn is sound, but 'good name/reputation' is a generic idiom, the adjectives and verbs differ, and the contexts (court advice vs. a Spartan speech) only loosely match.

Anchor (Lazar p.2258 w3-w5) checked: the oath-sworn host raised their hands to heaven (hambarjeal ... zjer̄s ənd erkins) and prayed 'You, holy Father, creator of heaven and earth ... Son ... Spirit', a Trinitarian creed on the Gospel. Il. 15.371 (Nestor prays, stretching his hand to the starry sky, 'Zeus father') and Pindar Isthm. 6.41-42 (Telamon raising his hands to the sky, 'Zeus father') checked as described. jer̄n ~ kheir < *ǵhes-r- is sound, but raising the hands to heaven in prayer is a universal gesture, and the Armenian is liturgical/Biblical ('lifting up hands', Ps 134:2; 'Father' here is the Christian Father).

Anchor (Lazar p.2219 w1) checked: 'arkʻ ew kanaykʻ, cerkʻ ew tłaykʻ' (men and women, old and young) in an exhortation to prayer that goes on to quote Matt 18:19-20. Il. 15.683 ἀνέρες ἠδὲ γυναῖκες (spectators of the horse-vaulter) checked. Cognates are sound (ayr < *h2nēr, kin/kanaykʻ < *gwen-), but 'men and women' is an elementary merism found everywhere and is standard Biblical/Septuagint wording (ἄνδρες τε καὶ γυναῖκες, Acts 8:12), which the Armenian church register follows. Not diagnostic. The same pair recurs in the L008 anchor (ayr ew kin, w3).

Same Vahagn anchor as L002 (fire hair, flame beard mawrus). RV 10.23.4b índraḥ śmáśrūṇi háritā abhí pruṣṇute = Indra sprinkles/wets his tawny beard (with soma); 10.23.1c = shaking his beard, he rose upright. Loci checked and read as stated, but the context is Indra drinking soma, not fiery birth, and hári- is colour, not fire. mawrukʻ ~ śmáśru- (Martirosyan) is sound. The argument from Vahagn = Vərəθraγna ~ vṛtrahán Indra is a chain of inferences through Iranian. One cognate element with a colour attribute; a weaker partner than the Agni lines in L002.
known: Same as L002: the Vahagn song is a known comparandum for Vedic material.

reasons: Same Armenian maxim as L003 (one day of shown worth and death rather than a long life in disgrace). MBh 12.138.39-40 (one should blaze even for a moment like a tinduka torch, not smoulder long like chaff fire, naraḥ ciram) and 5.131.63-65 (Vidulā: do not smoke, blaze, even for a moment) checked; the lead's reading is accurate. The only cognate is the man word (ayr ~ nara- < *h2ner-), which is incidental. The Armenian lacks the blaze/smoke image that is the Sanskrit figure. Thematic only; generic heroic moralising.
known: The Vidulā exhortation (MBh 5.131) is often cited in comparisons of heroic ethics.

reasons: Anchor (Agathangelos p.1592) checked: 'since the fire of sins ate (eker hur meghacʻn) ... and God's wrath awoke'; Il. 23.182 (the fire eats twelve Trojan youths with you) checked. hur ~ pyr < *peh2ur is sound, but the verb's etymology is wrong: eker is the suppletive aorist ker- of utem, from *gwerh3- 'devour' (Martirosyan s.v. ker-), not *h1ed-; so the verb does not match ἐσθίει. 'Fire eats' is in any case natural, and the Armenian is Biblical (God as consuming fire, Deut 4:24; fire of sin and wrath).
known: Fire as eater (Gr. πῦρ ἔδει/ἐσθίει, Vedic Agni 'eater') is a known figure in IE poetics.

reasons: Anchor (Lazar p.2235 w1) checked: 'only one daughter (dustr), whom he had given in wifehood (tueal kanutʻean) to Hamazasp'. Il. 6.192 and 11.226 (he gave him his daughter) and Theog. 819 (gave Kymopoleia his daughter to wed) checked. The cognates are sound (dustr ~ thugater < *dhugh2ter; tam ~ didomi < *deh3-), but 'give one's daughter in marriage' is the ordinary expression in any patrilocal society, and 'tam ... kanutʻean' is also the standard Biblical Armenian rendering of 'give as wife' (δοῦναι εἰς γυναῖκα, Gen 29 etc.). Generic, not diagnostic.

Anchor (byliny 17662-17664) checked: a soldier's lament, 'pour, rain, moisten mother moist earth (мать сыру землю); open up, mother moist earth'. Lucretius 1.250-251 (rains that Father Aether casts into the lap of Mother Earth) and 2.992-993 (Mother Earth receives the drops of moisture) and AVŚ 1.2.1-2 (we know Parjanya as the reed's father, Earth as its mother) checked as described. Only the mother word is cognate (мать ~ mater ~ mātṛ́ < *meh2ter-); the earth words are three different lexemes (земля is cognate with χθών/kṣam-, not terra/pṛthivī). Rain fertilising Mother Earth is a real comparable complex, but Mother Earth is near-universal and areal; Lucretius follows Greek models (Euripides/Aeschylus), and the Russian is late folk song with no sky-father. Defensible as a topos, weak as wording.
known: Moist Mother Earth (мать сыра земля) and Sky Father / Earth Mother (Dyauṣ pitā-Pṛthivī mātā; Pater aether / Mater terra) are well-known topics in the literature.

reasons: Anchor (Lazar p.2346 w2) checked: Šapuh sends to the prince of Siwnikʻ, 'give a hand to my side (jer̄n tur yis kołmn)', i.e. come and help. Il. 23.75 (Patroclus' ghost: give me your hand, I lament, for I will not return) and Eur. Heracl. 307 (give them your right hand, children, as a pledge) checked: the Greek is a farewell or pledge handclasp, not military aid, so the contexts do not match. Cognates are sound (jer̄n ~ kheir; tam ~ didomi < *deh3-), but 'give a hand' is generic and can be calqued from Greek (cf. δοὺς χεῖρα, Acts 9:41).
